II-51.explain: LCH is a clonal myeloid neoplasm of Langerhans-type cells; HLH is not a tumour but uncontrolled immune activation by macrophages and T cells.
II-51.hook: LCH = Langerhans cells grow; HLH = Haemophagocytic LymphoHistiocytosis (hyperinflammation).

checks.q: Which cells are overactivated alongside macrophages in HLH?
checks.why: HLH = macrophages plus cytotoxic T cells; Langerhans cell proliferation defines LCH.

II-51.explain: LCH is driven by MAPK pathway mutations (BRAF V600E); HLH is either inherited (cytotoxicity genes) or triggered by infection or rheumatic disease.
II-51.hook: BRAF in LCH; EBV and sJIA (macrophage activation syndrome) trigger secondary HLH.

checks.q: Which mutation drives most LCH?
checks.why: BRAF V600E activates MAPK signalling in LCH; JAK2 is myeloproliferative, KIT is mastocytosis.

checks.q: Which virus classically triggers secondary HLH?
checks.why: EBV is the commonest infectious trigger of secondary HLH; systemic JIA is the rheumatic one.

II-51.explain: CD1a/langerin mark the Langerhans phenotype; in HLH, failed perforin killing means infected cells and immune cells are never cleared, so cytokines spiral.
II-51.hook: LCH cells: CD1a + CD207 (Birbeck granules). HLH: no perforin = no off-switch.

checks.q: Which markers are positive on LCH cells?
checks.why: CD1a and langerin (CD207) define Langerhans cells; CD34/CD117 are blast markers.

checks.q: Which defect underlies primary HLH?
checks.why: Perforin-mediated killing fails, so cytokine storm results; NADPH oxidase defect is CGD.

II-51.explain: LCH infiltrates bone (punched-out lesions), skin and pituitary; HLH looks like overwhelming sepsis with cytopenias and organomegaly.
II-51.hook: LCH triad (Hand-Schüller-Christian): skull lesions, DI, exophthalmos.

checks.q: Typical skull X-ray lesion in LCH?
checks.why: LCH gives lytic punched-out skull lesions; hair-on-end is thalassaemia/sickle cell.

checks.q: Pituitary LCH typically causes which endocrine problem?
checks.why: Posterior pituitary infiltration causes central DI, the commonest LCH endocrinopathy.

checks.q: Classic HLH clinical triad?
checks.why: HLH: fever, cytopenias and hepatosplenomegaly; the cytokine storm mimics sepsis.

II-51.explain: Liver, spleen and marrow involvement worsen LCH prognosis; HLH labs reflect macrophage activation (ferritin) and consumption (fibrinogen).
II-51.hook: HLH labs: ferritin sky-high, TG high, fibrinogen low.

checks.q: Which are the LCH 'risk organs'?
checks.why: Liver, spleen and marrow involvement define high-risk LCH; skin/bone are low-risk sites.

checks.q: Which fibrinogen level fits HLH?
checks.why: HLH: very high ferritin and triglycerides but low fibrinogen from consumption.

II-51.explain: Treatment scales with extent: one bone lesion can be curetted or watched; multisystem LCH needs chemo. HLH needs immune suppression, and inherited forms a new immune system.
II-51.hook: Single bone: scrape or wait. Familial HLH: transplant.

checks.q: Single bone LCH lesion usually needs?
checks.why: Unifocal bone LCH often resolves with curettage or observation; multisystem needs chemo.

checks.q: Definitive treatment of primary (familial) HLH?
checks.why: Familial HLH is a genetic cytotoxicity defect, so only HSCT cures it.

II-52.explain: Leukaemia is the commonest childhood cancer, but brain tumours are the commonest solid ones; in children they mostly sit below the tentorium (cerebellum/brainstem).
II-52.hook: Kids: tumours in the back (posterior fossa); adults: tumours on top.

checks.q: Commonest solid tumours of childhood?
checks.why: CNS tumours are the commonest solid tumours; leukaemia is the commonest cancer overall.

checks.q: Where do most childhood primary CNS tumours arise?
checks.why: Children's tumours are usually infratentorial, about half in the posterior fossa.

II-52.explain: Pilocytic astrocytoma is low-grade and curable by resection; medulloblastoma is malignant embryonal; ependymoma arises from ventricular lining.
II-52.hook: Pilocytic = Pleasant prognosis; Medullo = Malignant midline cerebellum.

checks.q: Commonest primary CNS tumour in children?
checks.why: Pilocytic astrocytoma is commonest with good prognosis; medulloblastoma is the commonest malignant.

checks.q: Childhood ependymoma typically arises where?
checks.why: Paediatric ependymoma is classically in the 4th ventricle floor.

checks.q: Turcot syndrome combines CNS tumours with?
checks.why: Turcot = FAP (or Lynch) + malignant brain tumours.

II-52.explain: A posterior fossa mass blocks the 4th ventricle outflow, causing hydrocephalus; medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so the whole neuraxis must be imaged.
II-52.hook: Medullo 'drops' down the spine via CSF.

checks.q: Posterior fossa mass leads to raised ICP mainly via?
checks.why: It blocks CSF outflow through the 4th ventricle → obstructive hydrocephalus.

checks.q: Cyst with a mural nodule suggests?
checks.why: Pilocytic astrocytoma = cyst plus enhancing mural nodule; medulloblastoma is solid midline.

II-52.explain: Lying flat overnight, CO₂ rises and dilates cerebral vessels, so ICP headache peaks on waking. Pineal masses press the tectum, impairing upgaze.
II-52.hook: Morning headache + vomiting = ICP until proven otherwise.

checks.q: When is raised-ICP headache typically worst?
checks.why: Nocturnal CO₂ retention causes vasodilatation, so headache peaks on waking.

checks.q: Parinaud syndrome features which gaze problem?
checks.why: Pineal compression of the dorsal midbrain → upward gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus.

II-52.explain: MRI of brain and whole spine stages drop metastases; LP with a mass and high ICP risks herniation. Histology and molecular markers refine type and risk.

checks.q: Key contraindicated test with raised ICP?
checks.why: LP with raised ICP risks coning; urgent MRI brain and spine instead.

checks.q: Perivascular pseudorosettes are typical of?
checks.why: Ependymoma = perivascular pseudorosettes; medulloblastoma = Homer-Wright rosettes, MYC amplification.

II-52.explain: Surgery debulks and relieves obstruction, steroids reduce oedema. Radiation harms the developing brain most in the very young, so it is delayed.
II-52.hook: Under 3: spare the brain from radiation.

checks.q: First-line approach for most childhood CNS tumours?
checks.why: Maximal safe resection plus dexamethasone and CSF diversion is the mainstay.

checks.q: Below which age is cranial radiotherapy avoided?
checks.why: Radiotherapy is avoided under ~3 years due to severe neurocognitive damage.

II-53.explain: Neuroblastoma comes from sympathetic neural crest (adrenal medulla, sympathetic chain); Wilms from embryonic kidney tissue that failed to mature.
II-53.hook: Neuro = nerve crest (adrenal); Wilms = kidney blastema.

checks.q: Neuroblastoma most often arises from?
checks.why: Sympathetic neural crest cells, most often in the adrenal medulla.

checks.q: Wilms tumour derives from which tissue?
checks.why: Wilms arises from metanephric mesenchyme (blastema); RCC is tubular epithelial.

II-53.explain: MYCN amplification drives aggressive neuroblastoma; Wilms is linked to WT1 deletion syndromes like WAGR (11p13).
II-53.hook: WAGR = Wilms, Aniridia, GU anomalies, Retardation.

checks.q: Strongest adverse prognostic marker in neuroblastoma?
checks.why: N-myc amplification predicts poor outcome; t(11;22) is Ewing.

checks.q: Which eye finding is part of WAGR?
checks.why: WAGR: Wilms, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, developmental delay.

II-53.explain: Neuroblastoma is a small round blue cell tumour forming rosettes around neurofibrils; Wilms spreads haematogenously to the lungs.

checks.q: Rosettes typical of neuroblastoma?
checks.why: Homer-Wright rosettes; Flexner-Wintersteiner are retinoblastoma.

checks.q: Commonest metastatic site of Wilms tumour?
checks.why: Wilms spreads most often to the lungs, so chest imaging is part of staging.

II-53.explain: Neuroblastoma children are often unwell with metastases (raccoon eyes, paraneoplastic dancing eyes); Wilms children look well with a smooth flank mass.
II-53.hook: Sick child + crossing mass = neuroblastoma; well child + flank mass = Wilms.

checks.q: Periorbital ecchymoses in neuroblastoma reflect?
checks.why: 'Raccoon eyes' come from orbital bone metastases.

checks.q: Wilms mass relation to the midline?
checks.why: Wilms is a smooth flank mass not crossing the midline; neuroblastoma often crosses.

II-53.explain: Any abdominal mass in a child is cancer until imaged; neuroblastoma secretes catecholamines, so urinary metabolites help diagnosis, and MIBG maps spread.

checks.q: First imaging for a child's abdominal mass?
checks.why: Same-day review and abdominal ultrasound; CT/MRI follow for staging.

checks.q: Raised urinary VMA and HVA suggest?
checks.why: Catecholamine metabolites VMA/HVA are raised in neuroblastoma, not Wilms.

II-53.explain: High-risk neuroblastoma needs multimodal intensive therapy plus anti-GD2 immunotherapy; SIOP shrinks Wilms first to reduce rupture, COG gets histology first.
II-53.hook: SIOP = Shrink first (chemo); COG = Cut first.

checks.q: Which immunotherapy target is used in high-risk neuroblastoma?
checks.why: Anti-GD2 antibodies target a neuroblastoma surface ganglioside.

checks.q: European SIOP Wilms approach begins with?
checks.why: SIOP gives chemo before surgery; US COG usually operates first.

II-54.explain: Osteosarcoma makes malignant bone during the adolescent growth spurt; Ewing is a neuroectodermal small round cell tumour; rhabdomyosarcoma comes from muscle precursors.

checks.q: Peak age of osteosarcoma?
checks.why: Osteosarcoma peaks at 10-20 years with the growth spurt.

checks.q: Commonest soft tissue sarcoma of childhood?
checks.why: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest paediatric soft tissue sarcoma.

II-54.explain: Ewing is defined by an EWSR1-FLI1 fusion; osteosarcoma follows loss of RB1 or TP53 and radiation; botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma is in young girls' vagina.

checks.q: Translocation of Ewing sarcoma?
checks.why: Ewing carries t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1; t(9;22) is Philadelphia.

checks.q: Which syndrome predisposes to osteosarcoma?
checks.why: Hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1), Li-Fraumeni and prior radiation predispose.

checks.q: Sarcoma botryoides typically affects?
checks.why: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (botryoides) presents as a vaginal mass in young girls.

II-54.explain: Osteosarcoma arises where bone grows fastest (metaphysis around the knee) and makes osteoid; Ewing favours the diaphysis. Both spread first to the lungs.

checks.q: Osteosarcoma usually arises in which bone region?
checks.why: Metaphysis of long bones, often around the knee.

checks.q: Ewing sarcoma typically affects which region?
checks.why: Ewing: small round blue cells in the diaphysis, e.g. femur.

checks.q: Commonest metastatic site of bone sarcomas?
checks.why: Lungs are the commonest metastatic site, so chest CT is needed.

II-54.explain: Bone pain with swelling, especially at night, is a red flag; Ewing can cause fever and raised markers mimicking infection. Grapes from the vagina are botryoid sarcoma.
II-54.hook: Night bone pain + swelling = image it.

checks.q: Osteosarcoma presentation?
checks.why: Painful enlarging mass, bone pain with swelling, pathological fracture.

checks.q: Ewing sarcoma may mimic which condition?
checks.why: Fever, pain and swelling in Ewing can mimic osteomyelitis.

checks.q: Soft tissue lump above what size needs urgent US?
checks.why: Lump >2 cm, deep, enlarging or painful → urgent ultrasound.

II-54.explain: Aggressive periosteal reactions on X-ray hint at the tumour; muscle markers confirm rhabdomyosarcoma, and core biopsy gives tissue without spreading tumour.

checks.q: Onion-skin periosteal reaction suggests?
checks.why: Onion-skin = Ewing; sunburst and Codman triangle = osteosarcoma.

checks.q: Rhabdomyoblasts stain for?
checks.why: Desmin and myogenin are muscle markers; CD99 is Ewing.

II-54.explain: Osteosarcoma resists radiation so surgery plus chemo is key; Ewing responds to radiation, which can replace surgery in difficult sites.

checks.q: Radiotherapy response of osteosarcoma?
checks.why: Osteosarcoma is radio-resistant: en bloc resection + chemotherapy.

checks.q: Ewing sarcoma radiosensitivity?
checks.why: Ewing is radiosensitive: chemo + surgery and/or radiotherapy.

checks.q: Soft tissue sarcoma treatment combines?
checks.why: Wide excision plus chemotherapy and radiation.

II-55.explain: Chemo kills rapidly dividing cells, cancerous or not, so it causes immediate toxicities and delayed damage to growing organs.

checks.q: Chemotherapy mainly targets which cells?
checks.why: Rapidly dividing cells, which explains early and late toxicities.

II-55.explain: Marrow, gut mucosa and hair follicles turn over fastest; topoisomerase II inhibitors cause characteristic 11q23 secondary leukaemias.

checks.q: Which tissue suffers most from chemo turnover toxicity?
checks.why: High-turnover tissues: marrow, mucosa, hair.

checks.q: Etoposide is linked to which second cancer?
checks.why: Etoposide (topo II inhibitor) causes secondary AML.

II-55.explain: Counts fall to their lowest 1-2 weeks after chemo; lysis of tumour cells floods the blood with intracellular K, phosphate and urate, and phosphate binds calcium.

checks.q: When is the marrow nadir after chemotherapy?
checks.why: Nadir 7-14 days → neutropenia and infection risk.

checks.q: Which electrolyte is low in tumour lysis syndrome?
checks.why: High K, phosphate, urate; calcium falls as it binds phosphate.

II-55.explain: Each drug has a signature organ toxicity; matching drug to organ is a high-yield exam pairing.
II-55.hook: Doxo = heart, Cis = ears/kidney, Cyclo = bladder, Vincristine = nerves, Bleo = lungs.

checks.q: Anthracyclines cause which cardiac problem?
checks.why: Anthracyclines → dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy.

checks.q: Haemorrhagic cystitis follows which drug?
checks.why: Cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide metabolite acrolein causes haemorrhagic cystitis.

checks.q: Bleomycin causes which toxicity?
checks.why: Bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis and mucositis.

II-55.explain: Neutropenic children may show only fever, so fever is treated as sepsis. Survivors need surveillance for organ damage and second cancers.

checks.q: First step in febrile neutropenia?
checks.why: Emergency: take cultures and start antibiotics immediately.

checks.q: Which is a recognised late effect of chemotherapy?
checks.why: Late effects: cardiac, gonadal, endocrine, neurocognitive, second cancers.

II-55.explain: Antibiotics within the golden hour save lives; specific antidotes protect specific organs. Rasburicase causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

checks.q: Antibiotic timing in febrile neutropenia?
checks.why: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.

checks.q: Mesna protects against toxicity of?
checks.why: Mesna binds acrolein from cyclophosphamide; dexrazoxane protects from anthracyclines.

checks.q: Which route makes vincristine fatal?
checks.why: Intrathecal vincristine causes fatal ascending neurotoxicity.

III-1.explain: T1DM is autoimmune loss of insulin; with no insulin, glucose spills into urine and the body burns fat, explaining the classic symptoms.
III-1.hook: 4 Ws: Wee, Wa(ter), Weight loss, Weary.

checks.q: Absolute insulin deficiency in T1DM results from?
checks.why: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction; insulin resistance is T2DM.

checks.q: Which weight change fits new T1DM?
checks.why: Classic four: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss despite good appetite, fatigue.

III-1.explain: Islet autoantibodies mark the autoimmune process; autoimmunity clusters, so coeliac and thyroid disease are screened for.

checks.q: Which autoantibody is typical of T1DM?
checks.why: GAD, IA-2, ZnT8 and insulin antibodies; anti-TPO is Hashimoto, anti-tTG coeliac.

checks.q: Commonest associated diseases in T1DM?
checks.why: Coeliac disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis (screening answer).

III-1.explain: Glucose drags water into urine (osmotic diuresis); fat breakdown makes ketoacids; serum K may look normal but total body K is depleted.

checks.q: Hyperglycaemia causes dehydration via?
checks.why: Glycosuria pulls water into urine → osmotic diuresis.

checks.q: Total body potassium in DKA is?
checks.why: Total body K⁺ is depleted even if serum K looks normal or high.

III-1.explain: Bedwetting in a dry child reflects polyuria; in DKA, deep sighing breaths blow off CO₂ to compensate the acidosis.
III-1.hook: Kussmaul = deep breaths to blow off acid.

checks.q: New bedwetting in a dry child suggests?
checks.why: Secondary enuresis is a classic polyuria sign in new diabetes.

checks.q: Breathing pattern in DKA?
checks.why: Deep Kussmaul breathing compensates metabolic acidosis.

III-1.explain: A child with symptoms and high glucose can deteriorate to DKA within hours, so same-day specialist referral is needed. DKA needs glucose, acidosis and ketones.

checks.q: Symptoms + glucose 18.2 mmol/L: next step?
checks.why: Refer immediately to a paediatric diabetes centre (screening answer).

checks.q: DKA glucose threshold?
checks.why: DKA: glucose >11 mmol/L, venous acidosis and ketones.

III-1.explain: Fluids first, then low-dose insulin without a bolus to lower osmolality slowly and avoid cerebral oedema. Pumps with sensors are the most modern T1DM therapy.
III-1.hook: No bolus, go slow: protect the brain.

checks.q: Starting insulin infusion dose in DKA?
checks.why: 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h, no bolus (screening answer).

checks.q: Leading cause of death in paediatric DKA?
checks.why: Cerebral oedema (headache, bradycardia) → mannitol or 3% saline.

checks.q: Most modern T1DM therapy?
checks.why: Insulin pump with an integrated glucose sensor (screening answer).

III-2.explain: Metabolic syndrome clusters insulin-resistance consequences around central obesity; T2DM teens are obese, antibody-negative and still make plenty of insulin (high C-peptide).
III-2.hook: T2 teen: fat, antibody-free, C-peptide high.

checks.q: Metabolic syndrome requires central obesity plus how many criteria?
checks.why: Central obesity + ≥ 2 of high TG, low HDL, HTN, high fasting glucose.

checks.q: C-peptide in paediatric T2DM?
checks.why: T2DM: insulin resistance with high C-peptide; autoantibodies negative.

III-2.explain: Puberty physiologically raises insulin resistance, adding to obesity and genetics. MODY is a single-gene, dominant diabetes in non-obese families.

checks.q: Which is a major T2DM risk factor in teens?
checks.why: Central obesity, puberty, family history and ethnicity drive T2DM.

checks.q: MODY inheritance?
checks.why: MODY is autosomal dominant, often 3 generations, not obese.

III-2.explain: Visceral fat releases free fatty acids that blunt insulin action; compensatory hyperinsulinaemia stimulates skin and ovary, causing acanthosis and PCOS.

checks.q: Visceral fat mainly causes?
checks.why: Visceral fat → insulin resistance → hyperinsulinaemia and FFAs.

checks.q: Which skin sign reflects insulin resistance?
checks.why: Insulin resistance → acanthosis nigricans, fatty liver, PCOS.

III-2.explain: High insulin acts on skin growth receptors causing dark velvety folds; many teens are found on screening, with obesity-related comorbidities.

checks.q: Dark velvety skin of the neck is called?
checks.why: Thick dark velvety skin in neck/axillae = acanthosis nigricans.

checks.q: Typical T2DM presentation in teens?
checks.why: Often found on screening; occasionally DKA; raised ALT, sleep apnoea, SCFE.

III-2.explain: Obesity is common in T1DM too, so antibodies and C-peptide are checked in every case. Very early or mild stable diabetes points to monogenic forms.
III-2.hook: Diabetes <6 months old = genes, not autoimmunity.

checks.q: Which tests separate type 1 from type 2?
checks.why: Autoantibodies and C-peptide in every new case.

checks.q: Diabetes before which age needs genetic testing?
checks.why: Diabetes <6 months is neonatal/monogenic → genetic testing.

III-2.explain: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity; insulin is needed for ketosis or very high HbA1c. HNF1A-MODY responds to sulfonylureas; GCK-MODY is benign.

checks.q: First-line drug in T2DM without ketosis?
checks.why: Metformin plus lifestyle; insulin if ketosis or HbA1c ≥ 8.5%.

checks.q: Which MODY is very sensitive to sulfonylureas?
checks.why: HNF1A-MODY responds to sulfonylureas; GCK-MODY needs no treatment.

checks.q: When should T2DM complication screening start?
checks.why: T2DM complications appear early, so screen from diagnosis.

III-3.explain: Central DI lacks ADH; nephrogenic DI has ADH but the kidney ignores it. Either way, the kidney cannot concentrate urine.
III-3.hook: Central = no signal; nephrogenic = deaf kidney.

checks.q: Nephrogenic DI is defined as?
checks.why: Central = deficient vasopressin; nephrogenic = renal resistance.

checks.q: Urine in DI is typically?
checks.why: DI causes dilute polyuria; glucose-rich polyuria is diabetes mellitus.

III-3.explain: Anything damaging the hypothalamus/pituitary stalk causes central DI; nephrogenic DI is inherited (V2 receptor) or from drugs/electrolytes.
III-3.hook: Nephrogenic: Lithium, high Ca, low K.

checks.q: Commonest tumour causing central DI in children?
checks.why: Craniopharyngioma, germinoma and LCH are classic central causes.

checks.q: Which drug causes nephrogenic DI?
checks.why: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI; carbamazepine can cause SIADH.

III-3.explain: ADH acting on V2 inserts aquaporin-2 channels to reabsorb water; without them, free water is lost and plasma becomes concentrated.

checks.q: Which channel is missing in the collecting duct in DI?
checks.why: ADH via V2 inserts aquaporin-2; absent → dilute urine.

checks.q: Infants with DI risk which electrolyte disorder?
checks.why: Free water loss without access to water → hypernatraemic dehydration.

III-3.explain: Large-volume urine at night and new bedwetting; thirst drives craving for cold water. Infants cannot drink on demand, so they fail to thrive and get fevers.

checks.q: Polyuria threshold in children?
checks.why: Polyuria >2 L/m²/day, nocturia, secondary enuresis.

checks.q: Which drink do DI patients characteristically prefer?
checks.why: Intense thirst with preference for cold water.

III-3.explain: High plasma osmolality with dilute urine proves DI; desmopressin response distinguishes a missing hormone from a deaf kidney; central DI needs imaging.
III-3.hook: Desmopressin works = central; no response = nephrogenic.

checks.q: Urine osmolality threshold confirming DI with high plasma osm?
checks.why: High plasma osm with urine osm <300 mOsm/kg confirms DI.

checks.q: Desmopressin concentrates urine >50% in?
checks.why: Central DI responds; nephrogenic does not.

checks.q: Central DI next investigation?
checks.why: MRI looks for craniopharyngioma, germinoma, LCH.

III-3.explain: Replace ADH in central DI but avoid water overload; thiazides paradoxically reduce urine in nephrogenic DI. Slow sodium correction prevents cerebral oedema.

checks.q: Main risk of desmopressin therapy?
checks.why: Desmopressin plus free drinking → hyponatraemia.

checks.q: Which diuretic treats nephrogenic DI?
checks.why: Thiazides (with low-solute diet) paradoxically reduce urine volume.

checks.q: Maximum hypernatraemia correction rate?
checks.why: ≤ 0.5 mmol/L/h to avoid cerebral oedema.

III-4.explain: The anterior pituitary makes six hormones; the posterior stores hypothalamic vasopressin. Disorders are deficiency or excess of either part.
III-4.hook: Anterior 'FLAT PiG': FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, Prolactin, GH.

checks.q: Which hormone is released by the posterior pituitary?
checks.why: Posterior pituitary releases vasopressin (and oxytocin).

III-4.explain: Midline brain malformations disrupt pituitary development; acquired causes damage the hypothalamic-pituitary region.

checks.q: Which congenital defect is linked to hypopituitarism?
checks.why: Midline defects: septo-optic dysplasia, cleft palate, single central incisor.

checks.q: Commonest acquired tumour cause of hypopituitarism in children?
checks.why: Craniopharyngioma; also irradiation, trauma, histiocytosis.

III-4.explain: GH deficiency slows growth but bones mature late too, keeping proportions normal. Craniopharyngioma sits above the sella and presses the chiasm crossing fibres.

checks.q: Bone age in GH deficiency?
checks.why: GHD: low growth velocity, delayed bone age, normal proportions.

checks.q: Craniopharyngioma visual field defect?
checks.why: Chiasm compression → bitemporal hemianopia.

III-4.explain: Newborn hypopituitarism: no GH/cortisol → hypoglycaemia; no gonadotrophins → micropenis. Cushing makes children fat but short, unlike simple obesity.
III-4.hook: Fat + slowing height = Cushing; fat + tall = simple obesity.

checks.q: Newborn hypopituitarism sign in boys?
checks.why: Hypoglycaemia, micropenis and prolonged jaundice.

checks.q: Weight gain with falling height velocity suggests?
checks.why: Simple obesity speeds height; Cushing slows it.

checks.q: Posterior pituitary disorders include DI and?
checks.why: Posterior: DI (deficiency) or SIADH (excess).

III-4.explain: Low IGF-1 screens for GHD; GH is pulsatile, so two failed stimulation tests are needed before imaging. Craniopharyngioma has calcified cysts.

checks.q: How many failed GH stimulation tests confirm GHD?
checks.why: Low IGF-1 → two failed GH stimulation tests → pituitary MRI.

checks.q: Craniopharyngioma imaging appearance?
checks.why: Suprasellar cystic calcified mass.

III-4.explain: Replace deficient hormones; thyroxine speeds cortisol breakdown, so giving it first can precipitate adrenal crisis. Dopamine agonists shrink prolactinomas.

checks.q: GH deficiency treatment continues until?
checks.why: Recombinant GH until final height.

checks.q: Which hormone is replaced before thyroxine?
checks.why: Thyroxine first can precipitate adrenal crisis; replace cortisol first.

checks.q: Prolactinoma first-line treatment?
checks.why: Dopamine agonist cabergoline shrinks prolactinomas.

III-5.explain: A block in cortisol synthesis means precursors are shunted into androgens; 21-hydroxylase is the step affected in almost all cases.

checks.q: Commonest adrenocortical enzyme defect?
checks.why: 21-hydroxylase causes ~95% of CAH (screening answer).

III-5.explain: CYP21A2 encodes 21-hydroxylase. In 11β deficiency, deoxycorticosterone builds up, acting as a mineralocorticoid → hypertension.

checks.q: Inheritance of CAH?
checks.why: Autosomal recessive CYP21A2 mutation.

checks.q: Which CAH form causes virilisation with hypertension?
checks.why: 11β: DOC excess gives hypertension plus androgens.

III-5.explain: Without cortisol feedback ACTH rises, enlarging the adrenals and pushing precursors into androgens; salt-wasters also lack aldosterone.

checks.q: ACTH level in CAH?
checks.why: Low cortisol → no negative feedback → ACTH up → hyperplasia.

checks.q: Hormonal pattern in salt-wasting CAH?
options: Low cortisol and aldosterone, high androgens
checks.why: Insufficient gluco- and mineralocorticoid, excess androgen (screening answer).

III-5.explain: Girls are spotted at birth by ambiguous genitalia; boys look normal and present in crisis at 1-3 weeks. Milder forms cause early pubic hair and growth spurt.
III-5.hook: Girls: genitals at birth. Boys: crisis week 1-3.

checks.q: How do girls with classic CAH present at birth?
checks.why: Girls show virilised genitalia at birth.

checks.q: Boys' salt-wasting crisis typically occurs at?
checks.why: Salt-wasting crisis at 1-3 weeks.

checks.q: Simple virilising CAH presents as?
checks.why: Androgen excess → peripheral precocious pseudopuberty.

III-5.explain: 17-OHP is the substrate before the block, so it accumulates; it is measured on newborn screening. Karyotype confirms sex in ambiguous genitalia.

checks.q: Diagnostic marker of 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
checks.why: Raised 17-OHP; ACTH and renin also high.

checks.q: Which test establishes genetic sex in ambiguous genitalia?
checks.why: Karyotype, pelvic ultrasound and CYP21A2 genetics.

III-5.explain: Crisis: replace cortisol, sodium and glucose fast. Long term: replace both hormone types, add salt in infancy, and increase steroids during illness.
III-5.hook: Sick day = double dose; carry the card.

checks.q: First drug in adrenal crisis?
checks.why: IV hydrocortisone, 0.9% saline 10-20 mL/kg and IV dextrose.

checks.q: Which mineralocorticoid is given long-term?
checks.why: Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone + salt in infancy.

checks.q: What is required during illness?
checks.why: Stress-dose steroids in illness; carry an emergency card.

III-6.explain: Hypothyroidism can be inborn or acquired; hyperthyroidism in children is nearly always Graves, driven by TSH-receptor antibodies.

checks.q: Commonest cause of childhood hyperthyroidism?
checks.why: Graves (Basedow) disease, driven by TRAb.

III-6.explain: Most congenital hypothyroidism is a gland that failed to form or migrate; maternal iodine lack transiently starves the newborn thyroid; Hashimoto dominates acquired cases.

checks.q: Commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism?
checks.why: Dysgenesis (~85%), most often an ectopic gland.

checks.q: Maternal iodine deficiency causes what in the newborn?
checks.why: Temporary primary hypothyroidism (screening answer).

checks.q: Commonest acquired hypothyroidism in children?
checks.why: Hashimoto thyroiditis is commonest.

III-6.explain: Thyroid hormone drives metabolism, bone maturation and brain myelination; stimulating antibodies mimic TSH and drive overproduction.

checks.q: Bone age in hypothyroidism?
checks.why: Slowed growth and development → delayed bone age.

checks.q: What drives Graves thyrotoxicosis?
checks.why: TRAb stimulate the TSH receptor → overdrive.

III-6.explain: Congenital hypothyroidism is subtle (jaundice, sluggishness); Hashimoto causes a painless goitre with slow growth. Graves: hypermetabolism and eye signs.

checks.q: Which neonatal sign suggests congenital hypothyroidism?
checks.why: Prolonged jaundice, constipation, hypotonia, macroglossia, umbilical hernia.

checks.q: Hashimoto goitre is typically?
checks.why: Hashimoto: painless goitre with growth failure.

checks.q: Which eye sign belongs to Basedow's triad?
checks.why: Weight loss, tachycardia, Graefe sign (screening answer).

III-6.explain: Heel-prick TSH after the neonatal TSH surge catches primary congenital hypothyroidism; antibody profile separates Hashimoto from Graves.

checks.q: When is the newborn heel-prick TSH taken?
checks.why: Heel-prick TSH on day 3-5, after the physiological surge.

checks.q: Graves thyroid function pattern?
checks.why: Graves: suppressed TSH, high T4/T3, TRAb; Hashimoto: high TSH, low T4.

III-6.explain: Early levothyroxine protects the brain. Methimazole blocks synthesis, propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms; methimazole can cause agranulocytosis.
III-6.hook: Sore throat on methimazole = check neutrophils.

checks.q: Levothyroxine dose in congenital hypothyroidism?
checks.why: 10-15 µg/kg/day within the first 2 weeks.

checks.q: Why is propylthiouracil avoided in children?
checks.why: PTU causes severe hepatotoxicity; methimazole is preferred.

checks.q: Sore throat on antithyroid drugs requires?
checks.why: Exclude agranulocytosis with an urgent blood count.

III-7.explain: Bone matrix forms at the growth plate but cannot calcify, so bones soften and bend; breast milk is low in vitamin D.

checks.q: Commonest cause of rickets?
checks.why: Mostly vitamin D deficiency in unsupplemented breastfed infants.

III-7.explain: Little sun, dark skin and unsupplemented breast milk cause nutritional rickets; phosphate-wasting forms raise FGF23 or damage tubules.
III-7.hook: XLH: PHEX broken, FGF23 high, phosphate lost.

checks.q: Which risk factor favours nutritional rickets?
checks.why: Unsupplemented breastfeeding, dark skin, little sunlight.

checks.q: Which hormone is high in X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets?
checks.why: PHEX mutation → high FGF23 → renal phosphate wasting.

III-7.explain: Low vitamin D reduces gut calcium; PTH rises to defend calcium but wastes phosphate, so the Ca × P product falls and the growth plate cannot mineralise.

checks.q: PTH response in vitamin D deficiency?
checks.why: Low Ca absorption → PTH rises → phosphate wasting.

checks.q: Why can't the growth plate mineralise?
checks.why: Low calcium-phosphate product prevents mineralisation.

III-7.explain: Soft skull and swollen growth plates (costochondral junctions, wrists) and bending of long bones; young infants may present with hypocalcaemic seizures instead.

checks.q: Soft, ping-pong-ball skull in rickets is called?
checks.why: Craniotabes; also rachitic rosary, Harrison sulcus, wide wrists.

checks.q: Infants <6 months with rickets may present with?
checks.why: Young infants: seizures, tetany, laryngospasm from hypocalcaemia.

III-7.explain: Nutritional rickets: high PTH and very high ALP from active osteoblasts; XLH has a primary phosphate leak with normal PTH and calcium.
III-7.hook: XLH: phosphate low, everything else normal.

checks.q: ALP level in nutritional rickets?
checks.why: Phosphate low, ALP very high, PTH high.

checks.q: PTH in XLH?
checks.why: XLH: low phosphate with normal calcium and normal PTH.

checks.q: Typical X-ray of rickets metaphyses?
checks.why: Cupping, fraying and splaying of metaphyses.

III-7.explain: Routine 400 IU daily prevents rickets; treatment uses high-dose vitamin D with calcium; XLH needs phosphate with active vitamin D or anti-FGF23. Magnesium is needed for PTH.

checks.q: Daily vitamin D prophylaxis for all infants?
checks.why: All infants receive 400 IU vitamin D daily.

checks.q: Minimum duration of high-dose vitamin D treatment?
checks.why: High-dose vitamin D ≥ 12 weeks plus calcium.

checks.q: Hypocalcaemia refractory to IV calcium: check?
checks.why: Hypomagnesaemia blocks PTH release and action.

III-8.explain: Autoantibodies to nuclear antigens form immune complexes that inflame many organs; childhood-onset SLE is more aggressive than adult SLE.

checks.q: Main mechanism of SLE?
checks.why: Immune complexes against nuclear antigens damage many organs.

checks.q: Childhood SLE severity compared with adults?
checks.why: cSLE in adolescent girls is more severe than adult disease.

III-8.explain: Oestrogen effects explain post-pubertal female predominance. Some drugs induce a milder lupus with anti-histone antibodies that remits on stopping.

checks.q: SLE is more common in which group?
checks.why: Female predominance after puberty; more common in non-white populations.

checks.q: Anti-histone antibodies suggest?
checks.why: Anti-histone: drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid).

III-8.explain: Immune complexes consume complement, so C3/C4 fall in flares. Maternal anti-Ro/La cross the placenta and damage the fetal conduction system.

checks.q: Complement levels in active SLE?
checks.why: Immune complexes consume complement → C3 and C4 fall.

checks.q: Maternal anti-Ro/La cause which neonatal problem?
checks.why: Anti-Ro/La damage the fetal conduction system → heart block.

III-8.explain: SLE hits skin, joints, serosa, kidneys, brain and blood. Nephritis is common in children and drives prognosis.

checks.q: SLE malar rash characteristically?
checks.why: Malar rash spares nasolabial folds; oral ulcers are painless.

checks.q: Frequency of nephritis in childhood SLE?
checks.why: Nephritis in 50-80% of cSLE, more than adults.

checks.q: Haemolysis in SLE is typically?
checks.why: Autoimmune Coombs-positive haemolysis, plus leucopenia, thrombocytopenia.

III-8.explain: ANA is sensitive (entry criterion); anti-dsDNA follows activity and kidney disease, anti-Sm is specific. CRP usually stays low in flares, so high CRP means infection.
III-8.hook: ANA = screen; Sm = specific; dsDNA = disease activity.

checks.q: Minimum ANA titre as SLE entry criterion?
checks.why: EULAR/ACR entry criterion: ANA ≥ 1:80.

checks.q: Most specific SLE antibody?
checks.why: Anti-Sm is most specific; anti-dsDNA tracks activity and nephritis.

checks.q: High CRP in febrile SLE suggests?
checks.why: CRP is usually low in flares; high CRP suggests infection.

III-8.explain: Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares in everyone; immunosuppression escalates with severity, up to cyclophosphamide/mycophenolate for nephritis and rituximab.

checks.q: Which drug does every SLE patient take?
checks.why: Hydroxychloroquine + sun protection for all.

checks.q: Moderate SLE steroid-sparing option?
checks.why: Moderate: azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate.

checks.q: Severe SLE induction starts with?
checks.why: IV methylprednisolone → mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide; rituximab if refractory.

III-9.explain: JDM is a vasculopathy hitting capillaries of muscle and skin. In children, scleroderma is usually localised to skin (linear), not systemic.

checks.q: Commonest idiopathic inflammatory myopathy in children?
checks.why: JDM is the commonest childhood myopathy.

checks.q: Commonest scleroderma type in children?
checks.why: Localised (linear) scleroderma; systemic sclerosis is rare.

III-9.explain: JDM is a disease of school-age children with female predominance.

checks.q: Peak age of JDM?
checks.why: JDM peaks at 5-10 years, more in girls.

III-9.explain: Complement-mediated capillary dropout causes ischaemia of muscle and skin. Unlike adults, JDM is rarely paraneoplastic.
III-9.hook: Adult DM: look for cancer; child DM: don't.

checks.q: What causes capillary loss in JDM?
checks.why: Complement deposition → capillary loss → weakness, rash, ulcers.

checks.q: Routine cancer screening in JDM?
checks.why: Rarely linked to malignancy in children, unlike adults.

III-9.explain: Proximal weakness makes children climb up their legs to stand; skin signs are pathognomonic; calcinosis is a late complication especially in children.
III-9.hook: Gottron on knuckles, heliotrope on lids.

checks.q: Which muscles are affected in juvenile myositis?
checks.why: Proximal limb muscles and neck flexors (screening answer).

checks.q: Red scaly papules over knuckles are?
checks.why: Gottron papules; heliotrope = purple eyelids.

checks.q: Which complication is commoner in JDM than adult DM?
checks.why: Calcinosis is much commoner in children.

III-9.explain: Muscle enzymes leak from damaged fibres; MRI shows oedema non-invasively; biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy. SSc antibodies help classify systemic disease.

checks.q: Which muscle enzyme is raised in JDM?
checks.why: CK, LDH, AST/ALT and aldolase rise; MRI shows oedema.

checks.q: Typical JDM muscle biopsy finding?
checks.why: Perifascicular atrophy; ragged red fibres are mitochondrial.

III-9.explain: Steroids control inflammation, methotrexate spares steroids; organ-specific therapy (CCB, ACEi) manages SSc complications.

checks.q: First-line JDM treatment?
checks.why: Steroids plus methotrexate; IVIG if severe.

checks.q: Localised scleroderma treatment?
checks.why: Methotrexate ± initial steroids plus physiotherapy.

checks.q: Drug for scleroderma renal crisis?
checks.why: ACE inhibitor for renal crisis; CCB for Raynaud.

III-10.explain: HSP is IgA immune-complex vasculitis of small vessels, mostly in early school-age children.

checks.q: Commonest vasculitis of childhood?
checks.why: HSP (IgA vasculitis) is commonest, ages 3-10.

III-10.explain: An infection primes IgA production, so HSP clusters after URTIs in colder months. Vessel size classifies other vasculitides.
III-10.hook: Takayasu big, Kawasaki medium, HSP small.

checks.q: HSP usually follows which preceding event?
checks.why: Follows URTI (often streptococcal), autumn and winter.

checks.q: Kawasaki disease is which vessel-size vasculitis?
checks.why: Takayasu large, Kawasaki medium, GPA small with c-ANCA.

III-10.explain: Vessel wall inflammation leaks blood despite normal platelets, giving palpable purpura. Gut wall oedema causes intussusception; renal IgA deposits cause nephritis.

checks.q: Platelet count in HSP?
checks.why: Palpable purpura with a normal platelet count, unlike ITP.

checks.q: Typical intussusception in HSP?
checks.why: HSP causes ileo-ileal intussusception; idiopathic is ileocolic.

III-10.explain: Gravity-dependent purpura is universal; joints and gut are commonly involved; kidneys usually show disease within the first weeks.

checks.q: Where is HSP purpura typically found?
checks.why: Palpable purpura on buttocks and lower legs.

checks.q: Arthritis frequency in HSP?
checks.why: Arthritis of ankles/knees ~75%; abdominal pain ~50-75%.

checks.q: When does HSP nephritis usually appear?
checks.why: Nephritis (~20-50%) usually within 4-6 weeks.

III-10.explain: Diagnosis is clinical: purpura is mandatory plus one other feature. Normal FBC/clotting excludes other bleeding causes; urine and BP screen kidneys.

checks.q: Which feature is mandatory for HSP diagnosis?
checks.why: Purpura is mandatory plus pain, IgA histology, arthritis or renal involvement.

checks.q: Coagulation tests in HSP?
checks.why: FBC and clotting are normal; check urine PCR and BP.

III-10.explain: HSP usually self-resolves: support and pain relief. Steroids ease gut pain but don't stop kidney disease, so follow-up urine and BP are essential.

checks.q: NSAIDs in HSP are allowed when?
checks.why: Supportive care; NSAIDs only if renal function is normal.

checks.q: Effect of steroids on HSP nephritis?
checks.why: Steroids treat severe abdominal pain but do not prevent nephritis.

checks.q: Duration of urine and BP monitoring in HSP?
checks.why: Monitor urine and BP for 6-12 months.
